title: Call to Adventure - It’s all About the Journey
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rULrrI9GfWU

Daniel (@dungeondive) admits he first dismissed Call to Adventure out of pique. He had spent a year working on his own dungeon crawler, which he wanted to name "Call to Adventure," and Chris and Johnny O'Neal got to market first. The game looked dull until Tom Vasel's review changed his mind. Now he loves it, just not as a competitive game. He plays it solo as a storytelling engine, "like a gaming tarot reader" sketching a hero's life in about thirty minutes.

He builds a character on camera. He picks Student over Merchant as the origin, Seeker of Truth as the motivation, and Blood of the Dragon over High Arcanist as the destiny. He explains the hero/antihero morality track and the dark runes that corrupt you while strengthening the adversary (here, the Dark Rider), and how three chapters of traits and challenges are resolved by casting runes.

Then he narrates the result. The adventurous student comes home to a burning city, barely survives, banishes the ghost of a loved one, investigates the fire from a mountain monastery, leads an expedition into darkness, and finally discovers the dragon's blood erupting from his own body while facing a sorceress. He readily admits the game itself isn't very strong, but the art rivals Gloom of Kilforth's and its atmosphere makes it one of his favourite games of the year.

----

Daniel happily ignores the scoring and plays Call to Adventure purely as a story generator. Do you have games you play "wrong" because the way you play them is more fun?
